claim: The locus coeruleus (LC) is the major source of central noradrenaline.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) projects throughout the brain and spinal cord and is the major source of central noradrenaline.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the LC.

claim: Activation of LC:SC module produced robust, lateralised anti-nociception.
source: Activation of the LC:SC module produced robust, lateralised anti-nociception while activation of LC:PFC produced aversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC produced aversion.
source: Activation of the LC:SC module produced robust, lateralised anti-nociception while activation of LC:PFC produced aversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: In a neuropathic pain model, LC:SC activation reduced hind-limb sensitisation.
source: In a neuropathic pain model, LC:SC activation reduced hind-limb sensitisation and induced conditioned place preference.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the neuropathic pain model.

claim: In a neuropathic pain model, LC:SC activation induced conditioned place preference.
source: In a neuropathic pain model, LC:SC activation reduced hind-limb sensitisation and induced conditioned place preference.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC exacerbated spontaneous pain in neuropathic pain model.
source: By contrast, activation of LC:PFC exacerbated spontaneous pain, produced aversion and increased anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC increased anxiety-like behaviour.
source: By contrast, activation of LC:PFC exacerbated spontaneous pain, produced aversion and increased anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Neuropathic pain has a population prevalence of 7–8%.
source: Neuropathic pain has a population prevalence of 7–8% (Bouhassira et al., 2008; Torrance et al., 2006) and remains difficult to treat (Finnerup et al., 2015) mandating research to improve therapies (von Hehn et al., 2012; Skolnick and Volkow, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Neuropathic pain remains difficult to treat.
source: Neuropathic pain has a population prevalence of 7–8% (Bouhassira et al., 2008; Torrance et al., 2006) and remains difficult to treat (Finnerup et al., 2015) mandating research to improve therapies (von Hehn et al., 2012; Skolnick and Volkow, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Many frontline treatments for neuropathic pain modulate spinal noradrenaline.
source: Many of the frontline treatments for neuropathic pain modulate spinal noradrenaline, either directly such as noradrenaline re-uptake inhibitors or as part of a common effector pathway such as gabapentinoids and opioids (Nakajima et al., 2012; Hayashida et al., 2007, 2008; Jasmin et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A functional deficit of noradrenergic control is associated with the development of sensitisation in neuropathic pain models.
source: A functional deficit of noradrenergic control is associated with the development of sensitisation in neuropathic pain models (Hughes et al., 2013; Hughes et al., 2015; De Felice et al., 2011; Xu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Current systemic pharmacological interventions commonly produce CNS side-effects such as anxiety, sleep disturbance, mood shifts and confusion.
source: However, current systemic pharmacological interventions to correct this imbalance commonly produce CNS side-effects such as anxiety, sleep disturbance, mood shifts and confusion, limiting their therapeutic utility (Finnerup et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published study.

claim: The locus coeruleus is the principal noradrenergic nucleus in the CNS.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) is the principal noradrenergic nucleus in the CNS (Dahlstroem and Fuxe, 1965) and is the main source of noradrenergic innervation to the spinal dorsal horn, forming part of a well-described analgesic circuit (Millan, 2002; Pertovaara, 2006; Howorth et al., 2009a; Bruinstroop et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The LC is the main source of noradrenergic innervation to the spinal dorsal horn.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) is the principal noradrenergic nucleus in the CNS (Dahlstroem and Fuxe, 1965) and is the main source of noradrenergic innervation to the spinal dorsal horn, forming part of a well-described analgesic circuit (Millan, 2002; Pertovaara, 2006; Howorth et al., 2009a; Bruinstroop et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The LC forms part of a well-described analgesic circuit.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) is the principal noradrenergic nucleus in the CNS (Dahlstroem and Fuxe, 1965) and is the main source of noradrenergic innervation to the spinal dorsal horn, forming part of a well-described analgesic circuit (Millan, 2002; Pertovaara, 2006; Howorth et al., 2009a; Bruinstroop et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The LC projects throughout almost the entire neuraxis.
source: The LC also projects throughout almost the entire neuraxis and plays a pivotal role in diverse behaviours such as learning and memory (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015), strategic behaviour (Tervo et al., 2014), motivation (Varazzani et al., 2015), and arousal (Sara and Bouret, 2012; Carter et al., 2010; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The LC plays a pivotal role in learning and memory.
source: The LC also projects throughout almost the entire neuraxis and plays a pivotal role in diverse behaviours such as learning and memory (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015), strategic behaviour (Tervo et al., 2014), motivation (Varazzani et al., 2015), and arousal (Sara and Bouret, 2012; Carter et al., 2010; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The LC plays a pivotal role in strategic behaviour.
source: The LC also projects throughout almost the entire neuraxis and plays a pivotal role in diverse behaviours such as learning and memory (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015), strategic behaviour (Tervo et al., 2014), motivation (Varazzani et al., 2015), and arousal (Sara and Bouret, 2012; Carter et al., 2010; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The LC plays a pivotal role in motivation.
source: The LC also projects throughout almost the entire neuraxis and plays a pivotal role in diverse behaviours such as learning and memory (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015), strategic behaviour (Tervo et al., 2014), motivation (Varazzani et al., 2015), and arousal (Sara and Bouret, 2012; Carter et al., 2010; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The LC plays a pivotal role in arousal.
source: The LC also projects throughout almost the entire neuraxis and plays a pivotal role in diverse behaviours such as learning and memory (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015), strategic behaviour (Tervo et al., 2014), motivation (Varazzani et al., 2015), and arousal (Sara and Bouret, 2012; Carter et al., 2010; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: LC-derived noradrenaline is causally linked to aversive states like stress, anxiety and depression.
source: Furthermore, LC-derived noradrenaline is also causally linked to aversive states like stress, anxiety and depression (McCall et al., 2015; Alba-Delgado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Drug treatments for chronic pain that globally enhance noradrenaline levels are likely to cause adverse effects by acting on LC neuronal circuits not directly involved in pain control.
source: Thus, drug treatments for chronic pain that globally enhance noradrenaline levels or mimic its action are likely to cause adverse effects by acting on LC neuronal circuits that are not directly involved in pain control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preceding discussion of LC functions and side effects.

claim: The LC has been characterised as a homogeneous cluster of neurons that provide a uniform global signal as part of a central arousal system.
source: The LC has been characterised as a homogeneous cluster of neurons that provide a uniform global signal as part of a central arousal system (Fuxe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published study.

claim: There is accumulating evidence for specialisation of the LC neurons into subsets on the basis of anatomical projections.
source: There is, however, accumulating evidence for specialisation of the LC neurons into subsets on the basis of: (1) anatomical projections (Loughlin et al., 1986; Kebschull et al., 2016; Chandler et al., 2014); (2) electrical properties (Chandler et al., 2014); and (3) co-transmitter content (Simpson and Lin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: There is accumulating evidence for specialisation of the LC neurons into subsets on the basis of electrical properties.
source: There is, however, accumulating evidence for specialisation of the LC neurons into subsets on the basis of: (1) anatomical projections (Loughlin et al., 1986; Kebschull et al., 2016; Chandler et al., 2014); (2) electrical properties (Chandler et al., 2014); and (3) co-transmitter content (Simpson and Lin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: There is accumulating evidence for specialisation of the LC neurons into subsets on the basis of co-transmitter content.
source: There is, however, accumulating evidence for specialisation of the LC neurons into subsets on the basis of: (1) anatomical projections (Loughlin et al., 1986; Kebschull et al., 2016; Chandler et al., 2014); (2) electrical properties (Chandler et al., 2014); and (3) co-transmitter content (Simpson and Lin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Distinct populations of LC noradrenergic neurons innervate the spinal cord (LC:SC) and prefrontal cortex (LC:PFC) based on anatomy and electrophysiology.
source: In accord with this organisational principle, we have demonstrated that distinct populations of LC noradrenergic neurons innervate the spinal cord (LC:SC) and prefrontal cortex (LC:PFC) based on anatomy and electrophysiology in vitro and in vivo (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: EGFP immunofluorescence was detected in 690 ± 38 neurons per LC after direct injection of lentiviral vector into the dorsal pons.
source: After transduction, EGFP immunofluorescence was detected in 690 ± 38 neurons per LC (N = 5) of which 98 ± 0.4% co-expressed dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH) confirming their identity as noradrenergic (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: 98 ± 0.4% of EGFP-positive neurons co-expressed dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH) confirming their identity as noradrenergic.
source: After transduction, EGFP immunofluorescence was detected in 690 ± 38 neurons per LC (N = 5) of which 98 ± 0.4% co-expressed dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH) confirming their identity as noradrenergic (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study confirming cell identity.

claim: PSAM-HA was detected in the membranes of 82/112 transduced LC neurons examined from three rats.
source: Subsequently, PSAM-HA was detected in the membranes of the LC neurons (Figure 1C, 82/112 transduced neurons examined from three rats).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: PSEM308 produced concentration-dependent inward currents of up to 800 pA in voltage clamp recordings from transduced LC neurons.
source: PSEM308 evoked concentration-dependent inward currents of up to 800 pA in voltage clamp (Vhold60 mV, 1–10 μM, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: PSEM308 (3 µM) increased firing frequency of transduced LC neurons eight-fold (0.54 ± 0.21 Hz to 4.22 ± 0.90 Hz).
source: Current-clamp recordings of transduced LC neurons showed an eight-fold increase in firing frequency (0.54 ± 0.21 Hz to 4.22 ± 0.90 Hz, Figure 1E) in response to PSEM308 (3 µM).
evidence: This is experimental data from current-clamp recordings.

claim: No response to PSEM308 (doses up to 10 μM) was detected in recordings from non-transduced LC neurons.
source: No response to PSEM308 (doses up to 10 μM) was detected in recordings from non-transduced LC neurons (n = 6).
evidence: This is experimental data serving as a negative control.

claim: There was no difference in intrinsic electrical properties between transduced and non-transduced LC neurons.
source: We found no difference in intrinsic electrical properties between transduced and non-transduced LC neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) suggesting that expression of PSAM is well tolerated.
evidence: This is experimental data comparing transduced and non-transduced neurons.

claim: Expression of PSAM is well tolerated by LC neurons.
source: We found no difference in intrinsic electrical properties between transduced and non-transduced LC neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) suggesting that expression of PSAM is well tolerated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of difference in electrical properties.

claim: Local pressure application of PSEM308 caused a time-locked and reproducible excitation in 12 out of 24 recorded LC units in PSAM expressing rats.
source: In PSAM expressing rats (N = 8), local pressure application of PSEM308, but not saline, caused a time-locked and reproducible excitation in 12 out of the 24 recorded units (Figure 1F), increasing their firing to 234% of baseline (2.63 ± 0.92 Hz to 6.15 ± 1.47 Hz).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vivo extracellular recordings.

claim: PSEM308 increased firing of responsive LC neurons to 234% of baseline (2.63 ± 0.92 Hz to 6.15 ± 1.47 Hz).
source: In PSAM expressing rats (N = 8), local pressure application of PSEM308, but not saline, caused a time-locked and reproducible excitation in 12 out of the 24 recorded units (Figure 1F), increasing their firing to 234% of baseline (2.63 ± 0.92 Hz to 6.15 ± 1.47 Hz).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vivo extracellular recordings.

claim: Six LC neurons showed a small reduction of their firing frequency (−34.6%, 2.83 ± 1.21 to 1.85 ± 0.86 Hz) in response to local PSEM308.
source: The remaining cells did not respond (n = 6) or showed a small reduction of their firing frequency (−34.6%, 2.83 ± 1.21 to 1.85 ± 0.86 Hz, n = 6) in response to local PSEM308 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vivo extracellular recordings.

claim: Inhibited LC units likely reflect LC neurons that are not themselves transduced but are inhibited by noradrenaline released from surrounding transduced and PSEM308-activated LC neurons.
source: These inhibited units, which were in some cases simultaneously recorded along with LC units whose activity was increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), likely reflect LC neurons that are not themselves transduced but are inhibited by noradrenaline released from surrounding transduced and hence PSEM308-activated LC neurons (as previously hypothesised by Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and supported by citation.

claim: Local application of PSEM308 did not alter baseline firing frequency in control LC neurons (2.99 ± 1.55 to 3.15 ± 1.58 Hz).
source: Local application of PSEM308 did not alter baseline firing frequency in control LC neurons (2.99 ± 1.55 to 3.15 ± 1.58 Hz, NS, n = 7 neurons from three non-transduced rats).
evidence: This is experimental data serving as a control.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of PSEM308 (10 mg/kg) increased LC discharge frequency 10-fold from 1.47 ± 0.93 to 14.76 ± 2.8 Hz after 20 min.
source: Intraperitoneal (i.p) injection of PSEM308 (10 mg/kg, same dose used throughout the rest of the study unless otherwise stated) increased discharge frequency 10-fold from 1.47 ± 0.93 to 14.76 ± 2.8 Hz after 20 min.
evidence: This is experimental data from in vivo recordings after systemic drug administration.

claim: LC neurons doubled their firing frequency after 5.9 ± 3.9 min following i.p. PSEM308 injection.
source: LC neurons doubled their firing frequency after 5.9 ± 3.9 min and cells reached their maximum discharge frequency after 15.9 ± 6.5 min (Figure 1G, median 15.8 Hz, range 10.5 to 27.2 Hz).
evidence: This is experimental data describing the time course of drug effect.

claim: LC neurons reached their maximum discharge frequency after 15.9 ± 6.5 min following i.p. PSEM308 injection.
source: LC neurons doubled their firing frequency after 5.9 ± 3.9 min and cells reached their maximum discharge frequency after 15.9 ± 6.5 min (Figure 1G, median 15.8 Hz, range 10.5 to 27.2 Hz).
evidence: This is experimental data describing the time course of drug effect.

claim: The evoked excitation outlasted the time of experimental recording (30 min) in four out of five neurons.
source: The evoked excitation outlasted the time of experimental recording (30 min) in four out of five neurons.
evidence: This is experimental data describing the duration of drug effect.

claim: High tonic LC discharge frequencies (5–10 Hz) are acutely aversive.
source: High tonic LC discharge frequencies (5–10 Hz) are acutely aversive (McCall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Conditioning with PSEM308 induced avoidance of the drug-paired environment in animals that bilaterally expressed PSAM in LC neurons.
source: Conditioning with PSEM308 induced avoidance of the drug-paired environment in animals that bilaterally expressed PSAM in LC neurons (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is experimental data from conditioned place preference testing.

claim: Avoidance was not seen with a lower dose of PSEM308 (5 mg/kg).
source: Such avoidance was not seen with a lower dose of PSEM308 (5 mg/kg), or in animals transduced with a control vector (LVPRS-EGFP ) and given PSEM308 (10 mg/kg).
evidence: This is experimental data showing dose-dependence.

claim: Avoidance was not seen in animals transduced with a control vector and given PSEM308 (10 mg/kg).
source: Such avoidance was not seen with a lower dose of PSEM308 (5 mg/kg), or in animals transduced with a control vector (LVPRS-EGFP ) and given PSEM308 (10 mg/kg).
evidence: This is experimental data serving as a control.

claim: LC:SC neurons play a role in anti-nociception.
source: Based on previous studies, we predicted that LC:SC neurons would play a role in anti-nociception (Jones and Gebhart, 1986; Howorth et al., 2009b) and hypothesised that the forebrain projecting LC neurons might play a different – potentially pro-nociceptive role (Hickey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a prediction based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Forebrain projecting LC neurons might play a potentially pro-nociceptive role.
source: Based on previous studies, we predicted that LC:SC neurons would play a role in anti-nociception (Jones and Gebhart, 1986; Howorth et al., 2009b) and hypothesised that the forebrain projecting LC neurons might play a different – potentially pro-nociceptive role (Hickey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on citation to a previous study.

claim: Bilateral injection of CAV2PRS-EGFP-2A-PSAM into the dorsal horn of the lumbar spinal cord transduced 380 ± 37 neurons in each LC.
source: Bilateral injection of CAV2PRS-EGFP-2A-PSAM into the dorsal horn of the lumbar spinal cord transduced 380 ± 37 neurons in each LC (N = 7, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data from retrograde transduction.

claim: LC:SC neurons were located in the ventral aspect of the nucleus.
source: These LC:SC neurons were located in the ventral aspect of the nucleus.
evidence: This is experimental observation from anatomical analysis.

claim: CAV2PRS-EGFP-2A-PSAM bilaterally injected into the PFC transduced 361 ± 72 neurons per LC.
source: In a second set of animals, CAV2PRS-EGFP-2A-PSAM bilaterally injected into the PFC transduced similar numbers of neurons (361 ± 72 per LC, N = 6).
evidence: This is experimental data from retrograde transduction.

claim: LC:PFC neurons were scattered throughout the LC with a more dorsal location than the LC:SC neurons.
source: However, these LC:PFC neurons were scattered throughout the LC with a more dorsal location than the LC:SC neurons (representing different groups of neurons as previously noted [Bruinstroop et al., 2012; Howorth et al., 2009a; Li et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is experimental observation from anatomical analysis supported by citations.

claim: 99.1 ± 0.5% of transduced LC:SC neurons were positive for DBH.
source: In both cases, the transduced LC:SC and LC:PFC neurons were positive for DBH (99.1 ± 0.5% and 99.1 ± 0.7%, respectively) indicating efficient and specific retrograde transduction of the noradrenergic neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data confirming cell identity.

claim: 99.1 ± 0.7% of transduced LC:PFC neurons were positive for DBH.
source: In both cases, the transduced LC:SC and LC:PFC neurons were positive for DBH (99.1 ± 0.5% and 99.1 ± 0.7%, respectively) indicating efficient and specific retrograde transduction of the noradrenergic neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data confirming cell identity.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LC:SC neurons significantly increased thermal withdrawal latency to radiant heat as compared to naive rats.
source: Chemogenetic activation of LC:SC neurons (PSEM308 i.p N = 7 rats) significantly increased thermal withdrawal latency to radiant heat as compared to naive rats (N = 6) (15 min post i.p., 10.3 ± 1.0 s LC:SC vs 7.5 ± 0.7 s naive, 30 min post i.p., 11.6 ± 0.9 s LC:SC vs 7.6 ± 0.2 s naive, 45 min post i.p., 10.1 ± 0.7 s LC:SC vs 7.3 ± 0.4 s naive [Figure 2B]).
evidence: This is experimental data from the Hargreaves' test.

claim: The time course of the anti-nociceptive effect (between 15 and 45 min post-dosing) is consistent with the kinetics of LC neuron activation after i.p PSEM308 injection.
source: This time course of the anti-nociceptive effect, between 15 and 45 min post-dosing, is consistent with the kinetics of LC neuron activation after i.p PSEM308 injection (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an inference linking behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claim: LC:SC anti-nociception was only seen in the hind-limb ipsilateral to the vector injection in the spinal cord.
source: Moreover, this LC:SC anti-nociception was only seen in the hind-limb ipsilateral to the vector injection in the spinal cord (Figure 2B), indicating an unexpected lateralised organisation of the LC:SC projection.
evidence: This is experimental data showing lateralized effect.

claim: The lateralised anti-nociception indicates an unexpected lateralised organisation of the LC:SC projection.
source: Moreover, this LC:SC anti-nociception was only seen in the hind-limb ipsilateral to the vector injection in the spinal cord (Figure 2B), indicating an unexpected lateralised organisation of the LC:SC projection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lateralized behavioral effect.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC neurons had no effect on the thermal withdrawal latency.
source: By contrast, activation of LC:PFC neurons had no effect on the thermal withdrawal latency.
evidence: This is experimental data from the Hargreaves' test.

claim: There is a functional dichotomy in the actions of the ascending and descending LC projections on acute pain.
source: This indicates a functional dichotomy in the actions of the ascending and descending LC projections on acute pain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrasting effects of LC:SC and LC:PFC activation.

claim: LC:SC neurons exhibited a lateralised projection to the spinal cord with a higher density of labelling on the side of the original CAV2 injection (Ipsilateral 62 ± 3.6% vs contralateral 26 ± 2.3%).
source: This showed that although ipsilateral spinal injection of CAV2PRS-EGFP-2A-PSAM labelled LC neurones on both sides, those neurones exhibited a lateralised projection to the spinal cord with a higher density of labelling seen on the side of the original CAV2 injection (Ipsilateral 62 ± 3.6% of DBH+ fibres also EGFP+ Vs contralateral 26 ± 2.3%, N = 4, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from anterograde tracing analysis.

claim: The lateralised spinal projection is in line with the lateralised anti-nociception noted after activation of the LC:SC.
source: This is in line with the lateralised anti-nociception noted after activation of the LC:SC (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference linking anatomical and behavioral findings.

claim: The LC:PFC showed very sparse projection of axons to the spinal cord.
source: In contrast, the LC:PFC showed very sparse projection of axons to the spinal cord but a high density was seen in cortical sites which was greatest in the PFC (53 ± 2.9% EGFP+/DBH+).
evidence: This is experimental data from anterograde tracing analysis.

claim: The LC:PFC showed high density of projection in cortical sites which was greatest in the PFC (53 ± 2.9% EGFP+/DBH+).
source: In contrast, the LC:PFC showed very sparse projection of axons to the spinal cord but a high density was seen in cortical sites which was greatest in the PFC (53 ± 2.9% EGFP+/DBH+).
evidence: This is experimental data from anterograde tracing analysis.

claim: The average spontaneous discharge frequency of WDR neurons was 1.86 ± 0.60 Hz.
source: The average spontaneous discharge frequency of WDR was 1.86 ± 0.60 Hz, that was increased to 16.52 ± 2.19 Hz by pinch stimulation of the hind paw.
evidence: This is experimental data from spinal dorsal horn recordings.

claim: Pinch stimulation of the hind paw increased WDR neuron discharge to 16.52 ± 2.19 Hz.
source: The average spontaneous discharge frequency of WDR was 1.86 ± 0.60 Hz, that was increased to 16.52 ± 2.19 Hz by pinch stimulation of the hind paw.
evidence: This is experimental data from spinal dorsal horn recordings.

claim: In LC:SC transduced animals, perfusion of PSEM308 (10 μM) inhibited the pinch-evoked discharge two-fold to 8.5 ± 1.8 Hz (12/14 WDR neurons).
source: In LC:SC transduced animals, perfusion of PSEM308 (10 μM) inhibited the pinch-evoked discharge two-fold to 8.5 ± 1.8 Hz (12/14 WDR neurons, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is experimental data from spinal dorsal horn recordings.

claim: Spontaneous firing and innocuous, brush-evoked discharge of WDR neurons were unaffected by PSEM308.
source: However, both spontaneous firing and innocuous, brush-evoked discharge were unaffected by PSEM308 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is experimental data from spinal dorsal horn recordings.

claim: Local activation of terminals of LC:SC neurons in the spinal cord causes a specific inhibition of nociceptive inputs to WDR neurons.
source: These data demonstrate that local activation of terminals of LC:SC neurons in the spinal cord causes a specific inhibition of nociceptive inputs to WDR neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing selective inhibition of pinch responses.

claim: Atipamezole (10 μM) prevented the LC:SC mediated-inhibition of the pinch response.
source: To address the question of whether the LC:SC inhibition of the pinch response was caused by spinal release of noradrenaline, Atipamezole (10 μM, α2-adrenoceptor antagonist) was co-applied with PSEM308 (10 μM). Atipamezole prevented the LC:SC mediated-inhibition of the pinch response (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is experimental data from pharmacological blockade experiment.

claim: Atipamezole alone had no effect on spontaneous discharge, evoked discharge after pinch or brush.
source: Atipamezole alone had no effect on spontaneous discharge, evoked discharge after pinch or brush indicating there is little ongoing spinal release of noradrenaline under anaesthesia (paired t-test p>0.05, n = 5 WDR neurons from two preparations, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is experimental data from control experiment.

claim: There is little ongoing spinal release of noradrenaline under anaesthesia.
source: Atipamezole alone had no effect on spontaneous discharge, evoked discharge after pinch or brush indicating there is little ongoing spinal release of noradrenaline under anaesthesia (paired t-test p>0.05, n = 5 WDR neurons from two preparations, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of atipamezole alone.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC caused avoidance of the drug-paired chamber in the CPP paradigm.
source: We found that activation of LC:PFC caused avoidance of the drug-paired chamber in the CPP paradigm indicating a negative affective valence (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data from conditioned place preference testing.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC indicates a negative affective valence.
source: We found that activation of LC:PFC caused avoidance of the drug-paired chamber in the CPP paradigm indicating a negative affective valence (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the avoidance behavior.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LC:PFC reduced centre time by 62.6% in the open-field test.
source: Chemogenetic activation of LC:PFC reduced centre time by 62.6% and doubled immobility time in the open-field test after PSEM308 i.p (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data from open-field testing.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LC:PFC doubled immobility time in the open-field test.
source: Chemogenetic activation of LC:PFC reduced centre time by 62.6% and doubled immobility time in the open-field test after PSEM308 i.p (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data from open-field testing.

claim: Activation of the LC:PFC neurons changes behaviour to produce anxiety/aversion and promoted immobility.
source: These findings indicate that chemogenetic activation of the LC:PFC neurons changes behaviour to produce anxiety/aversion and promoted immobility (as previously reported for high-frequency stimulation of the whole LC [Carter et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data and supported by citation.

claim: When the LC:SC neurons were transduced, conditioning with PSEM308 was not aversive in the CPP paradigm.
source: In contrast, when the LC:SC neurons were transduced, conditioning with PSEM308 was not aversive in the CPP paradigm (Figure 4A) and did not produce anxiety-like behaviour in the open-field test (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data from conditioned place preference testing.

claim: Activation of LC:SC did not produce anxiety-like behaviour in the open-field test.
source: In contrast, when the LC:SC neurons were transduced, conditioning with PSEM308 was not aversive in the CPP paradigm (Figure 4A) and did not produce anxiety-like behaviour in the open-field test (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data from open-field testing.

claim: There was no difference in the total distance animals travelled between drug or saline injection in the open-field test for LC:SC animals.
source: There was no difference in the total distance animals travelled between drug or saline injection in the open-field test for LC:SC animals (1894±90 PSEM308 vs 1885 ± 137 cm saline, paired t-test p=0.94) suggesting there was no gross locomotor deficit.
evidence: This is experimental data from open-field testing.

claim: There was no gross locomotor deficit from LC:SC activation.
source: There was no difference in the total distance animals travelled between drug or saline injection in the open-field test for LC:SC animals (1894±90 PSEM308 vs 1885 ± 137 cm saline, paired t-test p=0.94) suggesting there was no gross locomotor deficit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of difference in distance travelled.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of the LC:SC module does not produce the same negative affective behaviour that is seen with the LC:PFC module.
source: This indicates that chemogenetic activation of the LC:SC module does not produce the same negative affective behaviour that is seen with the LC:PFC module.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrasting behavioral effects.

claim: Tibial nerve transection causes progressive development of punctate mechanical hypersensitivity (von Frey threshold lowered from 16.0 ± 1.5 to 1.3 ± 0.3 g) over 3 weeks.
source: This procedure causes the progressive development of punctate mechanical (von Frey threshold lowered from 16.0 ± 1.5 to 1.3 ± 0.3 g, N = 15) and cold hypersensitivity (increased frequency of paw withdrawals from 10.6 ± 3.8 to 82.7 ± 3.8%, N = 15) over 3 weeks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the neuropathic pain model.

claim: Tibial nerve transection causes progressive development of cold hypersensitivity (increased frequency of paw withdrawals from 10.6 ± 3.8 to 82.7 ± 3.8%) over 3 weeks.
source: This procedure causes the progressive development of punctate mechanical (von Frey threshold lowered from 16.0 ± 1.5 to 1.3 ± 0.3 g, N = 15) and cold hypersensitivity (increased frequency of paw withdrawals from 10.6 ± 3.8 to 82.7 ± 3.8%, N = 15) over 3 weeks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the neuropathic pain model.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of the LC:SC module increased the mechanical withdrawal threshold after nerve injury (from 1.2 ± 0.3 baseline to 11.7 ± 3.3 g, 30 min after PSEM308 i.p).
source: Chemogenetic activation of the LC:SC module increased the mechanical withdrawal threshold after nerve injury (from 1.2 ± 0.3 baseline to 11.7 ± 3.3 g, 30 min after PSEM308 i.p, N = 6 (Figure 5B)).
evidence: This is experimental data from the neuropathic pain model.

claim: Activation of LC:SC produced a significant improvement in weight-bearing on the nerve-injured limb.
source: Similarly, we found that activation of LC:SC produced a significant improvement in weight-bearing on the nerve-injured limb, linking the reduced evoked mechanical hypersensitivity to a spontaneous behaviour (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the incapacitance test.

claim: Activation of the LC:SC had no effect on motor performance in rotarod testing of TNT animals.
source: Rotarod testing of TNT animals showed that activation of the LC:SC had no effect on motor performance indicating that these actions were not a consequence of motor impairment and reflected an analgesic action (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is experimental data from rotarod testing.

claim: The actions of LC:SC activation were not a consequence of motor impairment and reflected an analgesic action.
source: Rotarod testing of TNT animals showed that activation of the LC:SC had no effect on motor performance indicating that these actions were not a consequence of motor impairment and reflected an analgesic action (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of motor impairment.

claim: The chemogenetic analgesic effect on mechanical and cold allodynia was dose-dependent (1–10 mg/kg).
source: The chemogenetic analgesic effect on mechanical and cold allodynia was dose-dependent (1–10 mg/kg) and completely blocked by prior intrathecal (i.t) injection of the a2-adrenoceptor antagonist yohimbine (60 ng, 10.0 ± 2.6 g PSEM308 + vehicle to 1.2 ± 0.4 g PSEM308 + yohimbine, N = 5 (Figure 5D)).
evidence: This is experimental data showing dose-response relationship.

claim: The chemogenetic analgesic effect was completely blocked by prior intrathecal injection of yohimbine (60 ng).
source: The chemogenetic analgesic effect on mechanical and cold allodynia was dose-dependent (1–10 mg/kg) and completely blocked by prior intrathecal (i.t) injection of the a2-adrenoceptor antagonist yohimbine (60 ng, 10.0 ± 2.6 g PSEM308 + vehicle to 1.2 ± 0.4 g PSEM308 + yohimbine, N = 5 (Figure 5D)).
evidence: This is experimental data from pharmacological blockade experiment.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC module had no effect on evoked mechanical or cold responses in the nerve injury model.
source: In marked contrast to LC:SC, activation of the LC:PFC module by PSEM308 had no effect on evoked mechanical or cold responses in the nerve injury model and did not improve weight-bearing (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the neuropathic pain model.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC did not improve weight-bearing in the nerve injury model.
source: In marked contrast to LC:SC, activation of the LC:PFC module by PSEM308 had no effect on evoked mechanical or cold responses in the nerve injury model and did not improve weight-bearing (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the incapacitance test.

claim: Activation of the LC:SC neurones by systemic administration of PSEM308 (10 mg/kg) increased mechanical withdrawal thresholds after transduction 3 weeks post-nerve injury.
source: Activation of the LC:SC neurones by systemic administration of PSEM308 (10 mg/kg) increased mechanical withdrawal thresholds, attenuated cold allodynia and greatly reduced the incidence of spontaneous paw flinches (Figure 8B–D) much as we observed with pre-emptive transduction.
evidence: This is experimental data from the delayed transduction experiment.

claim: Activation of the LC:SC neurones attenuated cold allodynia after transduction 3 weeks post-nerve injury.
source: Activation of the LC:SC neurones by systemic administration of PSEM308 (10 mg/kg) increased mechanical withdrawal thresholds, attenuated cold allodynia and greatly reduced the incidence of spontaneous paw flinches (Figure 8B–D) much as we observed with pre-emptive transduction.
evidence: This is experimental data from the delayed transduction experiment.

claim: Activation of the LC:SC neurones greatly reduced the incidence of spontaneous paw flinches after transduction 3 weeks post-nerve injury.
source: Activation of the LC:SC neurones by systemic administration of PSEM308 (10 mg/kg) increased mechanical withdrawal thresholds, attenuated cold allodynia and greatly reduced the incidence of spontaneous paw flinches (Figure 8B–D) much as we observed with pre-emptive transduction.
evidence: This is experimental data from the delayed transduction experiment.

claim: The change in evoked responses after delayed transduction was blocked by intrathecal atipamezole (50 µg).
source: The change in evoked responses was blocked by intrathecal atipamezole (50 µg) indicating that it was mediated by spinal activation of a2- adrenoceptors (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is experimental data from pharmacological blockade experiment.

claim: The analgesic effect after delayed transduction was mediated by spinal activation of α2-adrenoceptors.
source: The change in evoked responses was blocked by intrathecal atipamezole (50 µg) indicating that it was mediated by spinal activation of a2- adrenoceptors (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the blockade by atipamezole.

claim: Post-hoc histology revealed an equivalent level of transduction of LC neurones following spinal CAV2 administration before or after TNT (CAV2 before TNT - 164.8 ± 38.1 vs CAV2 after TNT - 165.4 ± 25.5 neurons per animal).
source: Post-hoc histology for native EGFP revealed an equivalent level of transduction of LC neurones following the spinal CAV2 administration (CAV2 before TNT - 164.8 ± 38.1, N = 8 vs CAV2 after TNT - 165.4 ± 25.5 neurons per animal, N = 7).
evidence: This is experimental data from histological analysis.

claim: Nerve injury significantly increased the number of spontaneous foot-lifts over 5 min (6.2 ± 0.7 sham vs 30.7 ± 3.9 TNT).
source: As anticipated, we found that nerve injury significantly increased the number of spontaneous foot-lifts over 5 min (6.2 ± 0.7 sham, N = 6 vs 30.7 ± 3.9 TNT, N = 17 [Figure 7B + Video 1]).
evidence: This is experimental data from spontaneous pain behavior assessment.

claim: Activation of LC:SC more than halved the number of spontaneous foot-lifts in nerve injured rats (13.1 ± 2.9).
source: Activation of LC:SC more than halved the number of spontaneous foot-lifts in nerve injured rats (13.1 ± 2.9), consistent with a reduction of ongoing pain.
evidence: This is experimental data from spontaneous pain behavior assessment.

claim: Activation of LC:SC is consistent with a reduction of ongoing pain.
source: Activation of LC:SC more than halved the number of spontaneous foot-lifts in nerve injured rats (13.1 ± 2.9), consistent with a reduction of ongoing pain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduction in spontaneous pain behaviors.

claim: Activation of LC:PFC almost doubled the number of foot-lifts (52.6 ± 9.3).
source: By contrast, activation of LC:PFC neurons almost doubled the number of foot-lifts (52.6 ± 9.3 [Figure 7B]) suggesting a diametric modulation of spontaneous pain by these distinct subsets of LC neurons.
evidence: This is experimental data from spontaneous pain behavior assessment.

claim: The contrasting effects on foot-lifts suggest a diametric modulation of spontaneous pain by LC:SC and LC:PFC neurons.
source: By contrast, activation of LC:PFC neurons almost doubled the number of foot-lifts (52.6 ± 9.3 [Figure 7B]) suggesting a diametric modulation of spontaneous pain by these distinct subsets of LC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the opposing effects on spontaneous pain behaviors.

claim: In rats with neuropathic sensitisation, activation of LC:SC increased the time spent in the PSEM308-paired chamber.
source: In rats with neuropathic sensitisation, activation of LC:SC increased the time spent in the PSEM308-paired chamber, whereas LC:PFC activation induced aversion (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is experimental data from conditioned place preference testing in nerve injured animals.

claim: In rats with neuropathic sensitisation, LC:PFC activation induced aversion.
source: In rats with neuropathic sensitisation, activation of LC:SC increased the time spent in the PSEM308-paired chamber, whereas LC:PFC activation induced aversion (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is experimental data from conditioned place preference testing in nerve injured animals.

claim: The neuropathic animals obtain benefit from LC:SC activation.
source: These data indicate that the neuropathic animals obtain benefit from LC:SC activation but that their situation is worsened by LC:PFC activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the place preference data.

claim: The situation of neuropathic animals is worsened by LC:PFC activation.
source: These data indicate that the neuropathic animals obtain benefit from LC:SC activation but that their situation is worsened by LC:PFC activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the place preference data.

claim: There is a correlation between the PSEM308-induced modulation of chamber preference and the incidence of spontaneous foot-lifts across all groups of animals.
source: A link between the signs of ongoing pain and the affective component of pain is provided by the correlation between the PSEM308-induced modulation of chamber preference and the incidence of spontaneous foot-lifts across all groups of animals (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is experimental data showing correlation between measures.

claim: No correlation was found between chamber preference and PSEM308-induced changes in evoked responses.
source: No correlation was found between chamber preference and PSEM308-induced changes in evoked responses (data not shown) suggesting that modulation of ongoing pain is a better predictor of the perceived benefit of this intervention.
evidence: This is experimental data showing lack of correlation.

claim: Modulation of ongoing pain is a better predictor of the perceived benefit of this intervention than modulation of evoked responses.
source: No correlation was found between chamber preference and PSEM308-induced changes in evoked responses (data not shown) suggesting that modulation of ongoing pain is a better predictor of the perceived benefit of this intervention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential correlations.

claim: The effect on immobility caused by activation LC:PFC neurons was further enhanced by 135% by co-administration of reboxetine (1 mg/kg) (61.3 ± 8.0% PSEM308 to 82.8 ± 3.9% PSEM308 + reboxetine).
source: Furthermore, the effect on immobility caused by activation LC:PFC neurons was further enhanced by 135% by co-administration of reboxetine (1 mg/kg) (61.3 ± 8.0% PSEM308 to 82.8 ± 3.9% PSEM308 + reboxetine, N = 6) indicating that the effect was caused by release of noradrenaline.
evidence: This is experimental data from drug combination experiment.

claim: The effect of LC:PFC activation on immobility was caused by release of noradrenaline.
source: Furthermore, the effect on immobility caused by activation LC:PFC neurons was further enhanced by 135% by co-administration of reboxetine (1 mg/kg) (61.3 ± 8.0% PSEM308 to 82.8 ± 3.9% PSEM308 + reboxetine, N = 6) indicating that the effect was caused by release of noradrenaline.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhancement by reboxetine.

claim: PSEM308 application had no effect on open-field performance in LC:SC transduced or sham animals.
source: In contrast, PSEM308 application had no effect on open-field performance in LC:SC transduced or sham animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from open-field testing.

claim: In LC:SC transduced animals, the response of WDR units to all stimuli was reversibly attenuated by spinal application of PSEM308 (10 µM) in the TNT model.
source: In LC:SC transduced animals, the response of WDR units to all stimuli was reversibly attenuated by spinal application of PSEM308 (10 µM) and this effect was blocked by concurrent perfusion of atipamezole (10 µM) (Figure 6C+D).
evidence: This is experimental data from spinal dorsal horn recordings in nerve injured animals.

claim: The attenuation of WDR responses by PSEM308 was blocked by concurrent perfusion of atipamezole (10 µM) in the TNT model.
source: In LC:SC transduced animals, the response of WDR units to all stimuli was reversibly attenuated by spinal application of PSEM308 (10 µM) and this effect was blocked by concurrent perfusion of atipamezole (10 µM) (Figure 6C+D).
evidence: This is experimental data from pharmacological blockade experiment.

claim: In control, non-transduced, TNT rats PSEM308 was without effect on evoked responses in WDR neurons.
source: In control, non-transduced, TNT rats PSEM308 was without effect on evoked responses in WDR neurons (n = 8) (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data serving as a control.

claim: The spontaneous firing of the WDR neurons was unaffected by PSEM308 in the TNT model.
source: The spontaneous firing of the WDR neurons was unaffected by PSEM308 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is experimental data from spinal dorsal horn recordings in nerve injured animals.

claim: Local activation of terminals of LC:SC neurons in the spinal cord of nerve injured animals causes a α2-adrenoceptor-mediated inhibition of both responses to innocuous and noxious stimuli in WDR neurons.
source: These data demonstrate that local activation of terminals of LC:SC neurons in the spinal cord of nerve injured animals causes a a2-adrenoceptor-mediated inhibition of both responses to innocuous and noxious stimuli in WDR neurons (unlike in naïve animals where only responses to noxious stimuli were attenuated) but has no effect on spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from nerve injured animals.

claim: In naïve animals, only responses to noxious stimuli were attenuated by LC:SC activation.
source: These data demonstrate that local activation of terminals of LC:SC neurons in the spinal cord of nerve injured animals causes a a2-adrenoceptor-mediated inhibition of both responses to innocuous and noxious stimuli in WDR neurons (unlike in naïve animals where only responses to noxious stimuli were attenuated) but has no effect on spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is a comparison between nerve injured and naive animals.

claim: The inhibition of WDR responses is consistent with an inhibition of the afferent drives rather than a change in the excitability of the WDR neurons themselves.
source: This is consistent with an inhibition of the afferent drives rather than a change in the excitability of the WDR neurons themselves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of effects on WDR neurons.

claim: The LC:SC and LC:PFC neurons are distinct functional modules.
source: These two opposing actions of the LC:SC and LC:PFC neurons to either suppress nociceptive input or to produce negative affective responses reflects the fact that they are distinct functional modules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrasting functional effects.

claim: The distinct functional modules mirror their anatomical segregation.
source: This mirrors their anatomical segregation (Li et al., 2016) and implies that the modules could be capable of independent action, with recruitment in different behavioural contexts.
evidence: This is an inference linking functional and anatomical findings, supported by citation.

claim: The modules could be capable of independent action, with recruitment in different behavioural contexts.
source: This mirrors their anatomical segregation (Li et al., 2016) and implies that the modules could be capable of independent action, with recruitment in different behavioural contexts.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional organization.

claim: It may be the balance between recruitment of the 'restorative' LC:SC limb versus the 'alarmist' LC:PFC projection that determines whether pain following an injury resolves or persists into chronic pain.
source: We speculate that it may be the balance between recruitment of the 'restorative' LC:SC limb versus the 'alarmist' LC:PFC projection that determines whether pain following an injury resolves or persists into chronic pain (see also [Arora et al., 2016; Brightwell and Taylor, 2009; Taylor and Westlund, 2017]).
evidence: This is speculation about the role of LC modules in chronic pain, supported by citations.

claim: Recruitment of either module may actually reciprocally inhibit the other given the α2-adrenoceptor-mediated feedback inhibition within the locus coeruleus.
source: Further the recruitment of either module may actually reciprocally inhibit the other given the a2-adrenoceptor-mediated feedback inhibition within the locus coeruleus (Aghajanian et al., 1977).
evidence: This is speculation about reciprocal inhibition, supported by citation.

claim: Reciprocal inhibition would require each module to have different afferent drives that were independently regulated.
source: This would also require each module to have different afferent drives that were independently regulated.
evidence: This is speculation about the requirements for reciprocal inhibition.

claim: There is little evidence for independently regulated afferent drives to LC modules at present.
source: At present, there is little evidence for such an organisation but this is an emerging territory for which the necessary neurobiological toolboxes are only now being developed (Schwarz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The TRIO approach using CAV2 in combination with rabies vectors suggested that there was a distinction in the afferent innervation of the 'medullary projecting' LC neurons.
source: Their TRIO approach using CAV2 in combination with rabies vectors suggested that there was a distinction in the afferent innervation of the 'medullary projecting' LC neurons that we think likely represents collaterals from the LC:SC.
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference about the identity of the neurons.

claim: The TRIO findings provide preliminary evidence that input-output specialisation may be present within the LC.
source: This provides preliminary evidence that such an input – output specialisation may be present within the LC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited TRIO study.

claim: Previous studies using subtractive methods to study the role of the LC in pain regulation show subtle and sometimes contradictory effects on nociception.
source: Previous studies have employed subtractive methods to study the role of the LC in pain regulation in animal models. These methods using toxins, knock outs or lesions to inhibit the noradrenergic system typically show subtle and sometimes contradictory effects on nociception (Martin et al., 1999; Jasmin et al., 2003, 2002; Tsuruoka and Willis, 1996; Howorth et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The subtle and contradictory effects may be in part ascribed to long-term adaptation to the loss of a population of neurons.
source: This may be in part ascribed to the long-term adaptation to the loss of a population of neurons.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for contradictory findings.

claim: The LC is not a single functional entity with respect to pain regulation.
source: However, our findings of antithetical LC actions reported herein (and Hickey et al., 2014) provide an alternative explanation; namely that the LC is not a single functional entity with respect to pain regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and supported by citation.

claim: There are counterbalancing actions of individual LC modules.
source: Rather there are counterbalancing actions of individual modules and consequently the net effect of subtractive interventions will be difficult to predict/interpret.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of opposing actions.

claim: The net effect of subtractive interventions on the LC will be difficult to predict/interpret.
source: Rather there are counterbalancing actions of individual modules and consequently the net effect of subtractive interventions will be difficult to predict/interpret.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for experimental design.

claim: While some patients benefit from systemic dosing of noradrenaline re-uptake inhibitors, a majority either obtain no benefit or suffer side effects related to anxiety, changes in affect and sleep disturbances.
source: This consideration also applies to attempts to obtain therapeutic benefit from systemic dosing of noradrenaline re-uptake inhibitors in patients – while some benefit, a majority either obtain no benefit or suffer side effects that are often related to anxiety, changes in affect and sleep disturbances that are likely due to actions on ascending LC projections.
evidence: This is stated as clinical knowledge.

claim: Side effects from noradrenaline re-uptake inhibitors are likely due to actions on ascending LC projections.
source: This consideration also applies to attempts to obtain therapeutic benefit from systemic dosing of noradrenaline re-uptake inhibitors in patients – while some benefit, a majority either obtain no benefit or suffer side effects that are often related to anxiety, changes in affect and sleep disturbances that are likely due to actions on ascending LC projections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about LC:PFC.

claim: Targeting just the spinal projection could separate analgesia from many of the side effects.
source: Our findings indicate that targeting just the spinal projection could separate analgesia from many of the side effects.
evidence: This is an inference about therapeutic implications based on the findings.

claim: The LC has levels of sub-specialisation according to modalities.
source: In demonstrating this functional and anatomical dichotomy within the LC modules, we have provided behavioural evidence that indicates that the LC has levels of sub-specialisation according to modalities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of distinct functional modules.

claim: The organisation of the LC outputs into modules allows these influences in different behavioural contexts to be independently selected and regulated.
source: We speculate that the organisation of the LC outputs into modules allows these influences in different behavioural contexts to be independently selected and regulated.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of modular organization.

claim: The Locus Coeruleus would be more appropriately named Loci Coeruleus reflecting the fact that it appears to be a collection of noradrenergic modules.
source: Given this organisational structure, it may be that that the Locus Coeruleus would be more appropriately named Loci Coeruleus reflecting the fact that it appears to be a collection of noradrenergic modules each with distinctive paths and roles in regulating brain function.
evidence: This is speculation about nomenclature based on the findings.

claim: Co-administration of reboxetine amplified and prolonged the analgesic effect of PSEM308 and completely reversed mechanical hypersensitivity (17.8 ± 3.2 g) as compared to sham animals (17.9 ± 1.1 g).
source: Co-administration of reboxetine amplified and prolonged the analgesic effect of PSEM308 and completely reversed mechanical hypersensitivity (17.8 ± 3.2 g) as compared to sham animals (17.9 ± 1.1 g, [Figure 5C]).
evidence: This is experimental data from drug combination experiment.
